extracted.intended_audience: general readers, television/history enthusiasts, fans of comedy and broadcast history
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style historical and factual summary of a single television variety/comedy series, covering format, cast, musical guests, controversies, censorship, scheduling, cancellation, and legacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to contemporary youth viewership
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that appealed to contemporary youth viewership with daring political satire humor and significant popular music performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The series targeted the younger, more liberal generation (ages 15–25) and achieved major success despite being scheduled against NBC's Bonanza. Success attributed to socially relevant humor and popular musical acts (e.g., Buffalo Springfield, Pete Seeger, the Beatles, the Who).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pushing boundaries of permissible television satire
rubrics_metrics.description: The program extended the boundaries of what was considered permissible in television satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid evolution from a 'hip' version of a typical variety show to a show that tested limits of acceptable satire on TV — this creative risk led to frequent conflicts with network censors and ultimately contributed to disputes with CBS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-air delivery requirement (10 days)
rubrics_metrics.description: Network ordered that the Smothers deliver their shows finished and ready for air ten days before airdate so that the censors could edit the shows as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBS required pre-delivery for affiliate screening and censoring; failure to meet these contractual pre-air delivery dates was cited by network leadership as the reason for cancellation. Episodes not submitted on time could be refused for broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with network 'criteria of taste'
rubrics_metrics.description: Content was expected to conform to the standards or 'criteria of taste established by CBS.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Network executives exercised editorial control (deleting segments or lines). Examples: deletion of Belafonte segment tied to the 1968 DNC, cuts to satire of Bonanza, edits to Joan Baez's remarks about her husband. Network statements (e.g., Robert Wood) cited unwillingness to accept the brothers' content as a rationale for cancellation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser sensitivity affecting musical bookings
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of musical guests was constrained by the 'advertiser-sensitive nature of their music' or political affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite advertiser concerns, the show showcased artists other programs avoided (George Harrison, Joan Baez, Pete Seeger, Jimi Hendrix, etc.). Some performances were contested (Pete Seeger's 'Waist Deep in the Big Muddy' initially dropped over controversial verse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local affiliate edits and regional broadcast variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Local stations sometimes made their own deletions of controversial sketches or comments, causing variations in what audiences actually saw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by instances where local affiliates removed material independently; episodes could therefore air differently across markets, affecting reception and controversy management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and contractual consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractual disputes over delivery and content could lead to litigation and monetary remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After cancellation, the Smothers brothers filed a breach of contract suit; a federal court ruled in their favor in 1973 and ordered CBS to pay US$776,300 (with later contextualization of equivalent value). The dispute and its outcome are part of the show's legacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programming/scheduling strategy as a measure of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Being scheduled against established major programs was a notable factor in evaluating the show's performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite airing opposite NBC's Bonanza, The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour was described as a 'major success,' indicating strong youth-oriented appeal and ratings resilience even against dominant competitors.
